title: "Design matrices"

A regression formula is converted into a numeric [**design matrix**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=133). Each row represents one observed MALD item; each column gives that item's multiplier for one coefficient.

We move from equation to data in two steps: first we derive the matrix product, then we inspect observed rows and the fitted values they produce.

The basic idea is bookkeeping. One item contributes a row $[1,F_i^c,D_i^c,P_i^c]$: the initial $1$ multiplies the intercept, and the remaining entries multiply the three slopes. A matrix stores one such row for every item. Matrix multiplication then repeats the same multiply and add calculation without changing its meaning. We inspect observed MALD rows and their fitted values below.

## From equations to a matrix

The [matrix primer](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd#vectors-matrices-and-covariance)
begins with scalar multiplication, then builds dot products and matrix-vector
products from repeated scalar operations. We use that same sequence here. For
item \(i\), the four scalar products in the MALD regression are

$$
\widehat y_i
=
1\widehat\beta_0
+F_i^c\widehat\beta_F
+D_i^c\widehat\beta_D
+P_i^c\widehat\beta_P.
$$

The design row and coefficient vector collect the four multipliers and four
coefficients:

$$
\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & F_i^c & D_i^c & P_i^c
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\widehat\beta_0 & \widehat\beta_F & \widehat\beta_D & \widehat\beta_P
\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf T}.
$$

Their dot product abbreviates the four multiplications and their sum:

$$
\widehat y_i=\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}.
$$

Stacking all item rows gives one such calculation per row. The complete MALD
regression can then be written

$$
\mathbf y=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon.
$$

With $n$ observed items and $p$ coefficients, $\mathbf y$ is $n\times1$, $\mathbf X$ is $n\times p$, $\boldsymbol\beta$ is $p\times1$, and $\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ is $n\times1$. The product $\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta$ is thus an $n\times1$ vector containing one fitted mean per item.

The dimension labels are a compatibility check. The inner dimensions in $(n\times p)(p\times1)$ agree, leaving the outer dimensions $n\times1$. If the number of columns in $\mathbf X$ differed from the number of coefficients, the requested row-by-column dot products would not be defined.

## Inspecting observed rows

We select the actual MALD items nearest three observed frequency quantiles. These rows expose how the formula becomes numbers without inventing predictor combinations.

```{r}
#| label: inspect-mald-design-matrix
library(ggplot2)

mald <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-items.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
mald$log_frequency_c <-
  mald$log_frequency_subtlex - mean(mald$log_frequency_subtlex)
mald$log_duration_c <- mald$log_duration - mean(mald$log_duration)
mald$n_phones_c <- mald$n_phones - mean(mald$n_phones)

fit <- lm(
  mean_log_rt ~ log_frequency_c + log_duration_c + n_phones_c,
  data = mald
)

targets <- quantile(
  mald$log_frequency_subtlex,
  c(.1, .5, .9) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
)
indices <- vapply(
  targets,
  function(target) which.min(abs(mald$log_frequency_subtlex - target)),
  integer(1)
)
observed_rows <- mald[indices, ]
X_observed <- model.matrix(fit, data = observed_rows)
matrix_prediction <- drop(X_observed %*% coef(fit))
r_prediction <- predict(fit, newdata = observed_rows)

stopifnot(
  length(unique(indices)) == length(indices),
  max(abs(matrix_prediction - r_prediction)) < 1e-12
)

cbind(
  observed_rows[, c("item", "mean_log_rt")],
  X_observed,
  matrix_prediction
)
```

For each displayed row, `model.matrix()` supplies the four multipliers $[1,F_i^c,D_i^c,P_i^c]$. Multiplying those values by `coef(fit)` and summing produces `matrix_prediction`. Its equality with `predict()` checks in code the dot product derived above.

```{r}
#| label: plot-mald-design-matrix-fit
#| fig-cap: "Observed MALD item means and their fitted multiple-regression values. The diagonal marks exact agreement."
mald$fitted_mean_log_rt <- fitted(fit)

ggplot(mald, aes(fitted_mean_log_rt, mean_log_rt)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey45", alpha = 0.35, size = 1.2) + # dqr-allow: plot-aesthetic
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, color = "#2C6E9B", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(
    x = "Fitted mean log reaction time",
    y = "Observed mean log reaction time"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The complete matrix contains `r nrow(model.matrix(fit))` rows and `r ncol(model.matrix(fit))` columns. Its first column is the intercept column. The other columns contain observed centered item properties.

## From squared error to the coefficient estimates

We now need to choose the coefficients that make the total squared discrepancy as
small as possible. Recall that a [derivative is a local rate of
change](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd#derivatives-as-local-rates-of-change).
With one coefficient, its derivative tells us whether a small increase in that
coefficient would raise or lower squared error. With several coefficients, we
collect one such derivative for each coefficient in a **gradient**. A zero
gradient means that no sufficiently small move in any single coefficient
direction lowers the criterion.

The scalar calculation supplies the pattern. If \(q(b)=(y-xb)^2\), then

$$
q'(b)=-2x(y-xb).
$$

For the complete data matrix, the same calculation is performed for all rows
and coefficients at once. We differentiate

$$
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)^\top
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)
$$

with respect to $\boldsymbol\beta$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q(\boldsymbol\beta)
&=\mathbf y^\top\mathbf y
-2\boldsymbol\beta^\top\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y
+\boldsymbol\beta^\top\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta,\\
\nabla Q(\boldsymbol\beta)
&=-2\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y
+2\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=
\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y,
$$

Setting the gradient to zero gives the **normal equations**, the system that a
least-squares coefficient vector must satisfy. The matrix
\(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X\) converts a coefficient vector into the left
side of that system. Calling this matrix **invertible** means that the conversion
can be undone in exactly one way. When it is invertible, multiplying both sides
by its inverse yields

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y.
$$

The zero gradient identifies a stationary point. To determine whether that
point is the minimum, differentiate the gradient once more. Recall that a
[**Hessian**](../statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy.qmd#hessian-as-local-curvature)
collects the second derivatives and describes local curvature. Here it is

$$
\nabla^2Q(\boldsymbol\beta)
=
2\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X.
$$

For any nonzero direction $\mathbf a$,

$$
\mathbf a^\top
(2\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)
\mathbf a
=
2\lVert\mathbf X\mathbf a\rVert^2.
$$

If the columns of $\mathbf X$ are linearly independent, then
$\mathbf X\mathbf a$ cannot equal zero for a nonzero $\mathbf a$. The displayed
quantity is therefore positive in every coefficient direction. We call such a
Hessian **positive definite**. The [projection figure](#fig-projection-fitted-residual)
below shows the corresponding geometry: the residual direction is perpendicular
to the fitted column space. Positive definiteness says that the squared error surface curves
upward away from the stationary point in every direction, so the solution above
is the unique minimum.

The same matrix estimate follows from the Gaussian probability model. Suppose

$$
\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf X,\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2
\sim
\mathcal N(\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\mathbf I).
$$

Conditional independence and common variance give the log likelihood

$$
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta,v)
=
-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac n2\log v
-\frac{1}{2v}
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)^\top
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta),
$$

where $v$ is a candidate value for $\sigma^2$. Its coefficient score is

$$
\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ell
=
\frac{1}{v}
\mathbf X^\top
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta).
$$

Setting that score to zero gives the same normal equations and thus the same
$\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}$. Differentiating with respect to $v$ gives

$$
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial v}
=
-\frac{n}{2v}
+
\frac{
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)^\top
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)
}{2v^2}.
$$

At the maximizing coefficients, its zero occurs at

$$
\widehat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{ML}}
=
\frac{
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})^\top
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
}{n}
=
\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{n}.
$$

The [one-predictor derivation](frequentist-linear-regression.qmd#deriving-the-estimates-from-a-gaussian-model)
works through the product likelihood, the variance maximum, and the distinction
between this maximum likelihood variance estimate and the residual variance
estimate with denominator $n-p$.

This formula is the several-coefficient counterpart of dividing the centered $x$--$y$ cross-product by the centered $x$ sum of squares in [simple least squares](frequentist-linear-regression.qmd#from-discrepancies-to-an-objective). The inverse untangles the ways in which the design columns vary together. The later discussion of [correlated predictors](correlated-predictors.qmd) asks what happens when that untangling is weakly supported.

```{r}
#| label: verify-mald-matrix-fit
X <- model.matrix(fit)
y <- mald$mean_log_rt
beta_by_matrix <- solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, y))

stopifnot(max(abs(beta_by_matrix - coef(fit))) < 1e-10)

data.frame(
  term = names(coef(fit)),
  lm_estimate = coef(fit),
  matrix_estimate = drop(beta_by_matrix)
)
```

The design matrix makes coefficient meaning auditable. It also exposes a failure:
if one column is an exact linear combination of others, distinct coefficient
vectors can produce the same fitted values. Then the inverse does not exist and
the normal equations do not determine a unique coefficient vector. The
[correlated predictor problem](correlated-predictors.qmd) returns to this issue with the observed MALD design.

Full column rank means that no nonzero change in the coefficient vector can leave every fitted value unchanged. Geometrically, OLS projects $\mathbf y$ onto the column space spanned by the declared predictor columns.

## Seeing a projection {#projection-as-fitted-plus-residual}

In a two-observation illustration, the model's column space can be drawn as a
line. The fitted vector is the point on that line closest to the observed
response vector. The remaining arrow is the residual vector, and its right
angle with the model line explains why no movement along that line can reduce
the squared distance further.

```{r}
#| label: fig-projection-fitted-residual
#| fig-cap: "A two-dimensional response vector decomposed into its projection onto a model line and a perpendicular residual."
#| fig-alt: "Coordinate plane with a sloped gray model line through the origin. A blue arrow runs from the origin to the fitted projection on that line. A black arrow runs from the origin to the observed response. An orange residual arrow connects the fitted point to the observed point at a right angle to the model line."
#| echo: false

projection_diagram <- data.frame(
  x = c(0, 0, 2), # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
  y = c(0, 0, 1), # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
  xend = c(1.4, 2, 1.4), # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
  yend = c(2.2, 1, 2.2), # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
  quantity = factor(
    c("Observed response", "Fitted projection", "Residual"),
    levels = c("Observed response", "Fitted projection", "Residual")
  )
)

ggplot() +
  geom_abline(slope = 0.5, intercept = 0, color = "grey65", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_segment(
    data = projection_diagram,
    aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend, color = quantity),
    arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(0.16, "cm")),
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.55, y = 1.15, label = "model column space",
           color = "grey35", size = 3.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.10, y = 2.35, label = "observed", size = 3.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.15, y = 0.85, label = "fitted", size = 3.4) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Observed response" = "black",
               "Fitted projection" = "#2C6E9B",
               "Residual" = "#B24C24")
  ) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-0.15, 3), ylim = c(-0.15, 2.6), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Response coordinate 1", y = "Response coordinate 2", color = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The observed vector in the figure is the sum of the fitted projection and the
residual. A real regression has one response coordinate per observation, so we
cannot usually draw its column space. The same perpendicular decomposition
still holds, and the later calculation of [leverage](leverage-and-influence.qmd) uses it to
ask which rows have the greatest capacity to move the projection.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. What does one row of $\mathbf X$ represent?
2. Why is the intercept column constant?
3. How does a row produce one fitted value?
4. What matrix property fails under exact collinearity?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. One row represents one observed MALD item and gives its multiplier for each coefficient. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. A constant column of ones makes its coefficient contribute the same intercept to every fitted item mean. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The inner product $\mathbf x_i^\mathsf T\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ multiplies each row entry by its coefficient and sums the products. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. $\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X$ loses full rank and becomes noninvertible under exact collinearity. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

We next use [contrast coding](coding-categorical-predictors.qmd) to construct design columns for a categorical predictor.
